clue.text: Capacity business for Apollo, say?

parts.note: capacity is room or volume, i.e. space
a business or trade is a craft

explanation.surface: Someone weighs the capacity and commercial side of an Apollo mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags Apollo as an example: the Apollo missions flew in such vehicles.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollo was the name of NASA's moon-landing vehicles, an example of a vessel built for flight beyond Earth.

clue.text: Hold up spy

indicators.note: in a down clue, up says the word for hold is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to hold something is to keep it

explanation.surface: A spy holds up proceedings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold up' looks like a phrase meaning delay, but 'up' turns KEEP round to make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy is to take a quick secret look.

clue.text: Teach Sunday school to be virtuous

indicators.note: to school is to train or drill, so the letters are knocked into a new shape

explanation.surface: Sunday school teaching aims to make children morally good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sunday school' reads as one phrase, but Sunday gives S and 'school' is a verb asking for TEACH plus S to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste describes someone pure and morally upright, a synonym of virtuous.

clue.text: Shorter class affair creates a hullabaloo

indicators.note: shorter tells us the following word is cut down, here losing its last three letters

parts.note: the word class taken as written before trimming
an amour is a love affair

explanation.surface: A brief classroom romance causes uproar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shorter' trims CLASS to CL (losing ASS); AMOUR, French for love, is a love affair.
explanation.definitionFit: A clamour is a loud noisy outcry, much the same as a hullabaloo or uproar.

clue.text: Some alluvial soil used as well

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some silt deposited by rivers is put to use too.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit across the end of 'alluvial' and the start of 'soil'.
explanation.definitionFit: Also is an adverb meaning in addition or too, a synonym of as well.

clue.text: Half of Sussex turned out in ripped Indian silk

indicators.note: this word is a container marker: it says one piece is placed inside the other, and the clue words of the pieces show which way round

parts.note: ripped means tore

indicators.note: turned out says those three letters are rearranged into a new order
half of the county name means its first three letters only

explanation.surface: Half the county of Sussex appears dressed in torn silk from India.
explanation.walkthrough: SUS, the first half of Sussex (an English county), 'turned out' becomes USS, which goes 'in' TORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tussore is a coarse brownish silk from wild silkworms of India.

clue.text: Ornate style of a letter-opener?

definitions.meaning: the most decorated of the classical orders of architecture, with acanthus-leaf capitals
a citizen of Corinth would open a letter addressed to them, such as Paul's epistles in the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone asks about the fancy design of a paper knife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter-opener' suggests a paper knife; in fact it is a recipient of St Paul's letters to the people of Corinth.
explanation.definitionFit: Corinthian is the name of the most ornate classical column order, and also a native of Corinth, recipient of Paul's Letters.

clue.text: Sort of fool, this unwanted third party

definitions.meaning: a fool is also a creamy fruit pudding, and one well-known kind is made with a green tart berry
the person who tags along with a courting couple

explanation.surface: Someone is called a kind of idiot for intruding on a couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool' is not an idiot but a British dessert of puréed fruit and cream; to 'play gooseberry' is British slang for being the odd one out with a couple.
explanation.definitionFit: A gooseberry fool is a classic British pudding, and a gooseberry is a chaperone or spare person spoiling a couple's privacy.

clue.text: One hangs from a palm just for fun

definitions.text: One hangs from a palm just for fun

parts.words: One hangs from a palm just for fun
parts.note: suggests a coconut or monkey in a tree, but the palm is a hand, from which a toy on a string dangles and spins

explanation.surface: Something dangles playfully from a palm tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm' suggests a tropical tree; it is the palm of the hand, from which a string toy drops and climbs back.
explanation.definitionFit: The toy is a spool on a string held in the hand and rolled down and up for amusement.

clue.text: Foot-long skeleton of emu starts a stir

indicators.note: to stir is to mix things up, so the preceding letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An emu sets off a commotion, with a skeleton as long as a foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' looks like a first-letters signal but is just fodder; 'stir' is the anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The metatarsus is the set of five bones in the middle of the foot, so a stretch of skeleton running the foot's length.

clue.text: Youths unanimous in commendation of Sylvia?

definitions.text: Youths unanimous in commendation of Sylvia?

parts.words: Youths unanimous in commendation of Sylvia?
parts.note: recalls Shakespeare's song 'Who is Silvia?' from The Two Gentlemen of Verona, which asks why all the young country lovers commend her

explanation.surface: Young men all agree in praising a girl named Sylvia.
explanation.walkthrough: The song runs 'Who is Silvia? what is she, That all our swains commend her?'
explanation.definitionFit: Young rustic lovers or suitors in pastoral poetry are called by this old word.

clue.text: Fell unconscious in den

parts.note: a fell is an animal's skin or pelt, i.e. a hide
someone knocked unconscious is out

explanation.surface: Someone collapsed senseless in their room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like the past tense of fall, but it is the noun for an animal's pelt.
explanation.definitionFit: A den is a secret lair or bolt-hole, a place for lying low.

clue.text: One measures humidity of the merry-go-round

indicators.note: round suggests the letters are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gauge measures how damp a fairground ride is.
explanation.walkthrough: The fairground ride reads as one item, but its last part, 'round', is the anagram signal and only what comes before it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hygrometer is an instrument for gauging the moisture content of the air.

clue.text: Romberg's desolate air?

parts.note: read literally, a tune for an empty arid wilderness; in fact the title of Sigmund Romberg's 1926 operetta

explanation.surface: A composer writes a bleak and lonely tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Sigmund Romberg wrote the operetta The Desert Song; 'air' is a tune and 'desolate' hints at arid wastes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Desert Song is Romberg's operetta set in Morocco, punning on a melody of the barren dunes.

clue.text: American divorcee leather in leather

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'American divorcee leather in leather', has 'leather' twice; the parse EX in TAN uses only one, so the clue appears corrupted and no source gives the printed text.

clue.text: Receptacle for party dips?

parts.note: sounds like a bowl for crisps and salsa, but the dips are lucky dips, prizes rummaged for in husks at a children's party

explanation.surface: A bowl to hold the sauces at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A bran tub is a British party game: small prizes are buried in bran and children dip in to draw one.
explanation.definitionFit: The container is a tub filled with cereal husks, from which guests pull wrapped gifts by lucky dip.

clue.text: Sailors in bar destroyed in fire

indicators.note: in puts the sailors inside the word for bar

parts.note: bar as in except means but
RN, the Royal Navy, stands for sailors

explanation.surface: Seamen in a pub are consumed by flames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but it is the preposition meaning except, BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something burnt has been consumed or charred by flames.

clue.text: Show, we hear, to look back on

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is judged by its sound, not spelling

parts.note: to look back on something is to review it

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a show they once saw.
explanation.definitionFit: A revue is a theatrical entertainment of sketches, songs and dances.

clue.text: Cut waste at sea

definitions.meaning: naval slang for rubbish or surplus

explanation.surface: Someone trims refuse while sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gash' is Royal Navy slang for rubbish, thrown overboard as waste.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long deep slash wound, and also sailors' slang for garbage.

clue.text: Last stopping-place for a drink, you could say

indicators.note: you could say signals that the word sounds the same when spoken

parts.note: beer is a drink

explanation.surface: A pub stop is one's final halt for refreshment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last stopping-place' sounds like a final pub, but it is the stand for a coffin before burial.
explanation.definitionFit: A bier is the stand on which a corpse or coffin rests before burial, its final resting point above ground.

clue.text: Plague resort?

definitions.meaning: to plague is to trouble persistently, as a ghost does

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a disease-stricken spot is a holiday destination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' looks like a noun but is a verb meaning to torment.
explanation.definitionFit: To haunt is to torment repeatedly; a haunt is a place someone frequents regularly.

clue.text: This jet arrived in yesterday from France

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for arrived inside the French word

parts.note: hier is the French for yesterday
ARR is the timetable abbreviation for arrived

explanation.surface: A jet landed from France yesterday.
explanation.walkthrough: The Harrier is the British vertical take-off jet fighter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Harrier is a well-known jump jet military aircraft.

clue.text: Turkey for motorists, caught and cut into three parts

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Turkey for motorists, caught and cut into three parts', gives TR and C but nothing for the remaining ISE/T letters; the clue appears cut short and no source gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Turkey for motorists, caught and cut into three parts

clue.text: A Roman's turn for a stroke, possibly

indicators.note: a turn here is a twist that reorders the letters

parts.note: taken as written, with the s counted

explanation.surface: It is a Roman's turn to row stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stroke' is the rower nearest the stern who sets the pace, so the stroke is one example of a rower.
explanation.definitionFit: The stroke is the crew member who sets the rowing rhythm, an example of a rower.

clue.text: Means of escaping the class system?

definitions.text: Means of escaping the class system?

parts.words: Means of escaping the class system?
parts.note: reads as social mobility, but the class is a school lesson, and the escape is skipping it

explanation.surface: A way to rise above social rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Class system' suggests social hierarchy; the classes are school lessons dodged by skiving.
explanation.definitionFit: Truancy is staying away from school without permission, avoiding lessons.

clue.text: Bar put out, being short

indicators.note: out signals the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub is closed briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrupt means curt or brusque in manner, i.e. short with someone.

clue.text: This festival is an eye-opener to Daisy

indicators.note: the opener of the word eye is its first letter

parts.note: an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A celebration opens a girl named Daisy's eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like a girl's name but is the flower; an aster belongs to the daisy family.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is the Christian spring feast of the Resurrection.

clue.text: Farm butter a penny more? What a swindle!

parts.note: a ram on a farm is something that butts
P is the abbreviation for penny

explanation.surface: Farm butter costing a penny more is a rip-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' is not dairy spread but one who butts, a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramp is British slang for a con or racket, especially overcharging.

clue.text: German king's fragrant oil

definitions.meaning: several German kings and emperors bore the name
a variant name for attar, essential oil of roses

explanation.surface: A German monarch's perfume.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto I was a German king and Holy Roman Emperor; otto is attar of roses, a scented oil.

clue.text: Short dean-quite a change!

indicators.note: a change signals the letters are altered into another arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dean is brief: what a turnaround!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' means lacking or insufficient, not brief.
explanation.definitionFit: Short in the sense of falling below what is needed, deficient.

clue.text: Fish-eater observed in Inverness

indicators.note: observed in says the letters can be seen sitting inside the next word

explanation.surface: A fish-eating creature is spotted in a Scottish city.
explanation.walkthrough: Inverness is a city in the Scottish Highlands, a fitting place to see one.
explanation.definitionFit: The erne is the sea eagle, a bird of prey that catches fish.

clue.text: Standing character?

definitions.meaning: one's status or repute in the eyes of others

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether a character is upright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing character' suggests a figure on stage, but both words are synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Repute or standing is the esteem one holds, also called one's character in a reference.
